messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mohammad was a 75-year-old man of South Asian descent who had been a potter for most of his life. He immigrated to America years ago as a refugee, fleeing the violent conflict that had ravaged his homeland. Mohammad’s past trauma continued to impact every aspect of his life, and he now sought help as his symptoms had become overwhelming. Mohammad's traumatic experiences began during a devastating period of unrest in his home country. At that time, government forces were actively hunting down and arresting individuals who spoke out against the regime. One fateful day, Mohammad was out on a routine visit to a local market when he witnessed several friends being taken away by authorities. The scene was horrific; the sounds of car engines roaring as they sped away with the captives still vividly etched in his mind. He tried to flee but found himself surrounded by police officers who ultimately arrested him and held him for days. The memory of that event remained fragmented, with disconnected pieces that didn't fit together. Mohammad couldn’t articulate it clearly; the images were more real than any other memories he had. The trauma of those moments haunted him whenever he heard car sounds or saw a police officer. He found himself constantly scanning his environment for signs of danger, always on edge. In an effort to cope with these triggers, Mohammad began avoiding situations that might evoke fear or discomfort. For instance, he stopped attending funerals and visiting cemeteries because they reminded him too much of the grief and loss he had experienced. He also avoided any positive events that could make him feel happy or hopeful, fearing it would only be a fleeting moment before more tragedy struck. Mohammad’s work as a potter was deeply affected by his trauma. The clay, which used to be his medium for expression and joy, now felt heavy and burdensome. His constant vigilance made it difficult to focus on his craft, and he began withdrawing from social interactions with fellow potters at the local community center. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him. Mohammad’s low coping skills meant that even the slightest upset could send him into a tailspin. His marriage also suffered as he became increasingly isolated and paranoid. His wife, who had always been supportive, found it challenging to understand his sudden changes in behavior. She worried about him but felt helpless when every attempt at conversation was met with silence or abrupt dismissal. Mohammad’s avoidance of conflict meant that any situation involving disagreement or confrontation was particularly distressing for him. Despite these challenges, Mohammad finally decided to seek help after a particularly distressing episode triggered by the sound of sirens while he was working on a piece in his studio. The memory overwhelmed him, and he realized he couldn’t continue living this way. He was certain that if he didn’t address his symptoms soon, they would only get worse. In therapy, Mohammad expressed his deepest fears: the constant vigilance, the belief that he was no longer capable of doing what once gave him purpose, and a pervasive sense of hopelessness. At the same time, he held onto a glimmer of hope that with help, he might regain some semblance of normalcy in his life. He wanted to be able to work without constant fear, to reconnect with his wife, and to engage more fully with life again. Mohammad’s journey was far from easy, but the first step towards healing had been taken. His therapist understood that addressing his trauma would involve helping him process fragmented memories and develop new coping strategies. Mohammad hoped for a future where he could look at the world without constant fear and rediscover joy in his beloved craft of pottery once more.
